toc.title: Cost tools and S3 cost control
Block and file storage, backup, transfer and practice

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Use Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost and Usage Reports, tags and consolidated billing
  • Choose the cheapest S3 storage class and lifecycle for an access pattern
  • Control EBS, EFS and FSx costs
  • Pick backup and archival strategies with sensible retention
  • Choose the lowest-cost way to move data into AWS storage

2Cost tools and S3 cost control

Running case

Lantern and Loom Trims the Storage Bill

  • Product images reach 40 TB, and most are rarely viewed
  • Nightly backups must be kept for seven years
  • Oversized and forgotten EBS volumes pile up
  • Partners pull large data sets and upload by SFTP
  • The storage bill has tripled: find and fix the waste

Cost Management Tools

Tool What it does
AWS Cost Explorer Visualize and analyze cost and usage: filter, group, 13 months of history, forecast ahead, savings recommendations
AWS Budgets Set limits for cost, usage, RI and Savings Plans; alert by email or SNS when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold; budget actions
Cost and Usage Report (CUR) The most detailed cost data, delivered to S3 by hour, day or month, with tags; query with Athena
  • All three read the same underlying billing data

Exam tip: See and slice costs: Cost Explorer. Get warned: Budgets. Line-item detail: the Cost and Usage Report.

Tags, Accounts and Consolidated Billing

  • A cost allocation tag is a key and value label that groups costs by project, team or application
  • Two kinds: AWS-generated and user-defined; activate them in the Billing console first
  • Active tags appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report, after up to 24 hours
  • Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations: one bill, combined usage for volume discounts, shared Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts, no extra fee
  • Use separate accounts per workload to track cost

Exam tip: Cost by team or project: activated tags. Lower rates across accounts: consolidated billing.

S3 Storage Classes

  • Standard: frequent access, no minimum duration
  • Intelligent-Tiering: unknown or changing patterns
  • Standard-IA: monthly access, 30-day minimum, retrieval fee
  • One Zone-IA: re-creatable data in one AZ
  • Glacier Instant Retrieval: quarterly access in milliseconds, 90 days
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval: minutes to hours, 90 days
  • Glacier Deep Archive: under once a year, 180 days

Exam tip: The colder the class, the cheaper the storage and the costlier the retrieval.

S3 Intelligent-Tiering and Lifecycle Rules

Approach How it works Use it when
Intelligent-Tiering Moves objects between tiers by access: Infrequent after 30 days, Archive Instant after 90 days; no retrieval fees; small monitoring fee Access is unknown or changing
Lifecycle rules Transition objects after a set age, and expire them; apply to existing and new objects Access declines predictably
  • Objects under 128 KB are not tiered; IA classes bill 128 KB minimum
  • Deleting early still bills the minimum duration

Exam tip: Predictable aging: lifecycle rules. Unpredictable access: Intelligent-Tiering.

S3 Glacier Retrieval and Archiving

Class Access Retrieval
Glacier Instant Retrieval Milliseconds Direct reads
Glacier Flexible Retrieval Restore first Expedited 1 to 5 min, Standard 3 to 5 hours, Bulk 5 to 12 hours
Glacier Deep Archive Restore first Standard within 12 hours, Bulk within 48 hours
  • Bulk is the cheapest way to restore, and free for Flexible Retrieval
  • Batch Operations restores many objects in one request
  • Objects stay in S3; the old separate Glacier service is not used for these

Exam tip: Cheapest archive and hours are fine: Deep Archive with Bulk retrieval.

S3 Cost Levers

  • Requester Pays: the requester pays requests and data download; the owner pays storage; requests must be authenticated
  • Fewer, larger uploads cost less in requests than many tiny ones; use multipart upload for big files
  • Expire incomplete multipart uploads and old versions with lifecycle rules
  • S3 Storage Lens shows usage across the organization and recommends savings
  • Storage Class Analysis advises when to move data to Standard-IA
  • Data into S3 is free; the main fees are storage, requests, retrieval and data out

Exam tip: Share data without paying for downloads: Requester Pays.

Block Storage Cost: EBS

  • gp3 lets you choose IOPS and throughput apart from size, so it usually beats gp2 on cost
  • HDD volumes (st1, sc1) are cheapest per GB for throughput or cold data, but cannot boot
  • Right-size volumes and delete unattached ones
  • Snapshots are incremental, so frequent snapshots store only changes
  • Snapshot Archive cuts storage cost by up to 75 percent for snapshots kept 90 days or longer
  • Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshot schedules and deletion, at no extra cost

Exam tip: Pay only for the performance used: gp3 for SSD, HDD for big sequential data.

3Block and file storage, backup, transfer and practice

File Storage Cost: EFS and FSx

Service Cost levers
Amazon EFS Lifecycle policies move files to Infrequent Access (30 days by default) and Archive (90 days); One Zone file systems cost less; Elastic throughput charges only for what you use
FSx for Windows File Server HDD storage for shares and home directories, SSD only when latency matters; Single-AZ costs less than Multi-AZ; scale storage, IOPS and throughput separately
  • Storage auto scaling: S3 and EFS grow and shrink by themselves; EBS and FSx are resized by you; turn on RDS storage autoscaling for databases

Exam tip: Shared files that are rarely read: EFS lifecycle to Infrequent Access or Archive.

Backup and Archival Strategy

  • Match frequency to the recovery point objective; incremental backups keep frequent copies cheap
  • AWS Backup plans move backups to cold storage and delete them after retention
  • Keep each copy only as long as rules require; set retention on automated backups and delete old manual snapshots
  • Long-term archives: S3 Glacier classes, optionally with Object Lock
  • Cross-Region and cross-account copies add storage and transfer cost: use them for what truly needs them
  • Test restores, not just backups

Exam tip: Cheapest compliant archive: cold storage class plus a lifecycle that expires it on schedule.

Moving Data into AWS at Low Cost [Verify live]

Method Best for
AWS DataSync Online bulk transfer from NFS, SMB and HDFS to S3, EFS, FSx; scheduled, verified
AWS Transfer Family Managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 into S3 or EFS, no servers
Storage Gateway Ongoing hybrid access with a local cache
Snow Family Offline devices for very large data or poor bandwidth
Direct Connect or VPN A steady link for continuing transfers (module 14)
  • Compare size divided by bandwidth: if the network would take weeks, ship a device
  • As of 5 November 2026: check which Snow Family devices are available

Exam tip: Online and scheduled: DataSync. Partners using SFTP: Transfer Family. Weeks of network: Snow.

Choosing the Cheapest Storage

Situation Choice
Unknown access pattern S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Aging data, predictable Lifecycle to IA then Glacier
Archive, read once a year, hours OK Glacier Deep Archive
Re-creatable data One Zone-IA
Database volume EBS gp3
Big sequential reads EBS st1
Shared files, rarely used EFS with lifecycle
Partners pay for downloads Requester Pays

Exam tip: Name the access pattern and the retrieval delay you can accept, then pick the tier.

What the Exam Asks: Cost-Optimized Storage

  • Which S3 class or lifecycle fits the access pattern
  • Which EBS or file option is cheapest for the load
  • Which backup and retention plan meets the rules
  • Which transfer service is cheapest for the volume
  • Which cost tool: Cost Explorer, Budgets, CUR, tags or consolidated billing

Exam tip: Look for the clues: rarely, unknown, hours, weeks, partners, shared.

Design Check: Lantern and Loom Trims the Storage Bill

Requirement Design
Old product images rarely viewed Lifecycle: Standard, then Standard-IA, then Glacier Instant Retrieval
Unknown access on new uploads Intelligent-Tiering
Seven-year backups AWS Backup with a cold-storage lifecycle, or Glacier Deep Archive
Oversized EBS volumes Right-size to gp3, delete unattached
Old EBS snapshots Snapshot Archive
Partners pull big datasets Requester Pays
Partners upload by SFTP Transfer Family
Who spent what Activated tags and Cost Explorer
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1New customer uploads at Lantern and Loom have unpredictable access: some are viewed daily, others never again. The team wants lower storage cost without retrieval fees or manual tiering. Which storage class fits?

  • AS3 Standard-IA
  • BS3 One Zone-IA
  • CS3 Intelligent-Tiering
  • DS3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Show the answer

Answer: C. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically as access changes, with no retrieval fees. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA charge for retrieval, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval needs restores before access.

S2Lantern and Loom must keep seven years of nightly backups for compliance. The data is almost never read, and a restore may take up to 12 hours. Which option gives the lowest storage cost?

  • AS3 Standard with versioning turned on
  • BS3 Glacier Deep Archive, reached through a lifecycle rule
  • CS3 One Zone-IA
  • DStandard-tier EBS snapshots of an idle volume
Show the answer

Answer: B. Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 class for data read less than once a year, and a standard restore finishes within 12 hours. Standard and One Zone-IA cost more per gigabyte, and EBS snapshots of an idle volume are not an archive.

S3Which TWO statements about cost allocation tags and consolidated billing are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • ACost allocation tags must be activated in the Billing console before they appear in Cost Explorer
  • BConsolidated billing adds a fee for each member account
  • CConsolidated billing combines usage across accounts to share volume discounts
  • DActivating a tag applies it to costs from before the activation
  • EThe Cost and Usage Report can only be produced once a month
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. Tags appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report only after activation, and consolidated billing combines usage so volume discounts and Reserved Instance or Savings Plans discounts are shared. Consolidated billing has no extra fee, and reports update through the month.

S4Partners download large data sets from Lantern and Loom's S3 bucket every day, and the company wants the partners to pay the request and download charges. What should it configure?

  • ARequester Pays on the bucket
  • BS3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
  • CA bucket policy that denies all requests from other accounts
  • DS3 Replication into each partner's account
Show the answer

Answer: A. With Requester Pays, the requester pays for requests and data download while the owner pays for storage; requests must be authenticated. Transfer Acceleration adds cost, and a deny policy blocks the partners.

S5Partners upload files by SFTP. Lantern and Loom wants no servers to manage, and the files must land in Amazon S3. Which solution fits?

  • AAn EC2 instance running an SFTP daemon, with a cron job copying to S3
  • BPre-signed S3 URLs emailed to each partner
  • CAWS DataSync agents installed at every partner site
  • DAWS Transfer Family with an SFTP server endpoint backed by S3
Show the answer

Answer: D. Transfer Family provides fully managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 endpoints that store files in S3 or EFS, with no servers to run. An EC2 daemon needs management, and the other options do not accept SFTP.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Tools Cost Explorer, Budgets, CUR, activated tags, consolidated billing
S3 colder class equals cheaper storage and costlier retrieval; Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access; lifecycle for aging
Block and file gp3, HDD for throughput, snapshot archive, EFS lifecycle
Backup match frequency to recovery point, expire on schedule
Transfer DataSync, Transfer Family, Snow for the very large
